text.p: Following are some of the major
events to have occurred on April 25 in history:
1284 - King Edward II of England born. King from 1307, it
was during his reign that Robert the Bruce of Scotland
decisively beat the English armies at Bannockburn (1314).
1408 - Ladislas of Naples occupied Rome.
1599 - Oliver Cromwell, English soldier and statesman, born.
He lead Parliamentary armies in the Civil War and, after the
overthrow of Charles I, became Lord Protector of England (1653).
1744 - Anders Celsius, Swedish astronomer who invented the
Celsius thermometer, died.
1769 - Sir Marc Isambard Brunel, British engineer and
inventor, born. He pioneered techniques of underwater tunnelling
and built the Thames Tunnel in London from Wapping to
Rotherhithe. It opened in 1843.
1792 - Jacques Pelletier, a highwayman, became the first person to be guillotined in France, on the Place de Greve in Paris.
1850 - Paul Julius Reuter, founder of the news agency that bears his name, used 40 pigeons to carry stock market prices between Brussels and Aachen.
1859 - Work began on the construction of the Suez Canal, under the direction of Ferdinand de Lesseps. It was opened 10 years later on November 16, 1869.
1862 - New Orleans fell to the Union fleet of Admiral David Farragut in the American Civil War.
1874 - Guglielmo Marconi, Italian physicist and inventor of radio telegraphy, born. His work earned him a share of the 1909 Nobel prize for physics. He also developed short-wave radio.
1898 - The U.S. Congress passed a joint resolution declaring war on Spain over Cuba.

1908 - Edward Egbert Roscoe Murrow, U.S. broadcaster and journalist, born. He was director of the U.S. Information Agency, and famous for his broadcasts from London during World War Two prior to American intervention.
1918 - Ella Fitzgerald, American jazz singer, born. Discovered at 16 at an amateur night at the Apollo Theatre in Harlem, she went on to work with Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Count Basie.
1925 - Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg became the second president of Germany's postwar Weimar Republic.
1926 - Arturo Toscanini conducted the first performance of Giacomo Puccini's opera "Turandot" at La Scala, Milan.
1945 - The U.S. and Soviet armies met in the east German city of Torgau as World War Two drew to a close in Europe.
1945 - The San Francisco Conference sponsored by China, Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States opened to set up a world body to succeed the defunct League of Nations.
1971 - 200,000 anti-Vietnam War protesters marched on Washington.
1974 - Portugal's authoritarian ruler Marcelo Caetano was overthrown in a military coup, surrendering to General Antonio de Spinola who became president the following month.
1975 - Portugal held its first free elections for 50 years, the Socialist Party under Mario Soares won most seats.
1976 - Elections took place in Vietnam for a National Assembly to reunite the two halves of the country.
1980 - A U.S. commando mission to rescue 53 American embassy hostages in Iran was abandoned in the desert with the loss of eight American lives when a helicopter collided with a tanker aircraft.
1982 - British troops recaptured South Georgia, part of the Falkland Islands, from occupying Argentine forces.
1989 - Japanese Premier Noboru Takeshita announced his resignation over the Recruit Affair, the country's biggest political scandal in decades.
1990 - Violeta Chamorro was sworn in as president of Nicaragua having defeated Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega.
1990 - The Hubble space telescope was released from the space shuttle Discovery and orbited 300 miles above the Earth.
1990 - Warders in riot gear stormed Manchester's Strangeways jail and forced rebel inmates to surrender after 25 days, ending Britain's longest prison siege.
1995 - Ginger Rogers, U.S. star of stage and screen, died at 83. Most famous for her film dance routines with Fred Astaire notably in "Flying Down to Rio", "Roberta" and "Top Hat".
1996 - A court in Gdansk, Poland dropped proceedings against General Wojciech Jaruzelski over the 1970 fatal shootings of 44 protesters by security forces when he was defence minister.
1996 - Spain's Supreme Court found no evidence that outgoing Socialist Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez had been involved in organising a "dirty war" against Basque ETA separatists.
